approachQuestion.prompt:
Supply Bundles

A workshop has one container of each numbered supply item. Given positive integer values `items` and a positive integer `target`, return every subset of item indices whose values sum exactly to `target`. Each index may be used at most once. Represent each bundle as its indices in increasing order; return each qualifying bundle once, in any order.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 24; 1 <= items[i] <= 1000; items contains no duplicate values; 1 <= target <= 24000. The result may contain exponentially many bundles. The input is not modified.

Example 1: items=[2,3,5,7], target=10 -> [[0,1,2],[1,3]].
Example 2: items=[4,6,9], target=5 -> [] (no item can be selected).
Example 3: items=[1,2,3], target=6 -> [[0,1,2]] (the only bundle uses every item).
Example 4: items=[7,2,3], target=5 -> [[1,2]]; skipping the first item must not skip later candidates. Example 5: items=[1,2,3,4], target=11 -> []; even with no result, every subset remains a candidate when the target exceeds the total.

options.text: Carry the next eligible index and the remaining target. Scan every later index once; when its value fits, append it, recurse from the following index with the reduced target, then remove it. If the value is too large, skip only that candidate and continue scanning. Emit a copied path when the remainder is zero.
options.feedback: The next index prevents reuse, and append/recurse/remove restores the path for each sibling. Positivity proves an overlarge candidate cannot belong to this bundle, but the input is unsorted, so later indices must still be checked.

options.text: Generate every subset of indices, compute its sum, and keep the subsets whose sum equals the target.
options.feedback: This returns the right set, but visits all subsets even when a partial path already reaches the target; that completion needs no further choices.

options.text: Sort the values from largest to smallest and keep each value that does not exceed the remaining target; return the chosen indices if the remainder reaches zero.
options.feedback: A locally largest fitting value can block a valid bundle. For items=[4,5,6], target=9, choosing 6 leaves 3 and returns no bundle, although indices [0,1] have values 4+5=9.

options.text: Carry the current index and remainder, but recurse with the same index after selecting an item so that the branch can continue until its sum reaches the target.
options.feedback: This can use one physical item repeatedly. For items=[3,8], target=6, it can report index 0 twice even though each index is available only once.

feedback.reason: Select each candidate independently: with positive values, an item larger than the remainder cannot appear in a valid bundle, but unsorted input means it is safe to skip only that item and continue the sibling scan. Copy completed paths before undoing them.
details: Keep a path of increasing indices, the next index that may be selected, and the remaining amount. If the remainder is zero, append a copy of the path and return. Otherwise scan each later index exactly once. For a value no larger than the remainder, append its index, recurse from the following index with that value subtracted, then remove the index. For a value larger than the remainder, skip only that candidate and continue the scan; because the input is not sorted, do not stop the loop. Increasing indices prevent reuse and give each subset one construction path.

Increasing indices give each subset one construction path and prevent reuse. Because items are unsorted, an item above the remainder is skipped without ending the sibling scan. Copy each completed path before undo changes it.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For `increasing-index-sum-search`, let n be the number of items and R be the total number of indices across all returned bundles (counting repeated indices in different bundles). Choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Each loop iteration, recursive call, and path append/remove takes constant time. Exclude the input and returned bundles; include the recursion stack, current path, and copying each bundle into the result.

options.text: O(2ⁿ + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(2ⁿ + R) time, O(2ⁿ + R) auxiliary space
O(n·2ⁿ + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Count the increasing-index search tree plus actual copied result entries.
details: Each candidate-loop iteration chooses one possible next index, so across the full increasing-index choice tree there is at most one such iteration per nonempty subset, plus one state per prefix. For the allowed distinct values items=[1,2,...,n] and target=n(n+1)/2+1 (at most 301 for n<=24), the target exceeds the total. Every remaining item therefore fits at every prefix, so the search visits all 2ⁿ subsets and emits no result. Copying emitted bundles adds R.

Each candidate-loop iteration chooses one possible next index, so across the full increasing-index choice tree there is at most one such iteration per nonempty subset, plus one state per prefix. For distinct allowed values items=[1,2,...,n] and target=n(n+1)/2+1, every subset is visited and no result is emitted. Copying emitted bundles adds R.

Every recursive state corresponds to a selected-index prefix, hence to a subset. Each loop iteration chooses one next index and therefore corresponds to a distinct nonempty subset; total states and candidate iterations are O(2ⁿ), not O(n·2ⁿ). This bound is attained up to constants for distinct allowed values items=[1,2,...,n] and target=n(n+1)/2+1: this target is above the sum and no larger than 301, within the input domain. At every prefix, every remaining value fits, so the search visits every subset although the result is empty. Copying all emitted paths adds Θ(R).
The increasing index strictly advances, so stack depth and mutable path length are at most n. Each result path is copied into output; output storage is excluded. No visited-subset table is retained.

Worst-case time and auxiliary space. Each candidate check, recursive transition, append/remove, and result-index copy has unit cost. The stack and mutable path count as auxiliary space; input and returned bundles do not.
“O(n + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: A target larger than the sum of all values makes the method visit all subsets while emitting nothing.
“O(2ⁿ + R) time, O(2ⁿ + R) auxiliary space”: The algorithm does not retain all subsets, and returned bundles are excluded from auxiliary space.
“O(n·2ⁿ + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This multiplies by n unnecessarily: summing candidate-loop iterations over the whole tree gives one iteration per possible nonempty subset, up to a constant.
